summary: This note describes the All-India Muslim League, a political party founded in the early 20th century in British India. It arose from a literary movement centered on Aligarh and figures such as Syed Ahmad Khan, and its advocacy for a Muslim-majority nation, Pakistan, contributed to the 1947 partition. Initially it focused on Indian Muslim civil rights and the interests of the upper and gentry classes, and it spent its early decades building organization and credibility.
one_line: The All-India Muslim League was an early 20th-century British Indian party that advocated a separate Muslim-majority nation, Pakistan.
key_facts: The All-India Muslim League, popularly called Muslim League, was a political party established during the early years of the 20th century in the British Indian Empire.
The Muslim League's strong advocacy for a separate Muslim-majority nation-state, Pakistan, successfully led to the partition of British India in 1947.
The party arose out of a literary movement begun at the Aligarh Muslim University, in which Syed Ahmad Khan was a central figure.
Sir Syed founded the Muhammadan Educational Conference in 1886.
The Muhammadan Educational Conference had a self-imposed ban that prevented it from discussing politics.
In December 1906, the Muhammadan Educational Conference in Dhaka, attended by 3,000 delegates, removed the ban.
The December 1906 Dhaka conference adopted a resolution to form an All Indian Muslim League political party.
The original political goal of the Muslim League was to define and advance the civil rights of Indian Muslims.
The Muslim League aimed to provide protection to the upper and gentry class of Indian Muslims.
From 1906 to the 1930s, the party worked on its organizational structure and its credibility in Muslim communities across the British Indian Empire.
The party lacked the character of a mass organisation during its early decades.
The Muslim League represented the landed and commercial Muslim interests of the United Provinces, today's Uttar Pradesh.
